newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - S&P deals blow to Thailand.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - S&P deals blow to Thailand.

text.p: In yet another body blow for Thailand, Standard & Poor's put its long-term foreign-currency and local-currency ratings on review for possible downgrade on Friday.
About US$3 billion worth of foreign currency debt is affected by the move, which S&P blamed on greater-than-expected loan losses in the Thai financial sector.
S&P said these loan losses would impose "a sizable fiscal burden on the government and weakened economic growth in the next several years".
"So far, Thailand's weak coalition government has been slow to recognise and effectively manage problems in the financial sector," it said.
"An erosion of investor confidence, in turn, has intensified balance of payment pressures and tight domestic liquidity conditions, despite the recent depreciation of the Thai baht."
This was the only reference to the baht in the statement, which focused on high corporate and household indebtedness and the cost of recapitalising Thai bank and finance companies.
The S&P review is expected to take one month.

Thailand's bank sector has been hit by a string of downgrades or negative reviews from rating agencies this year, and Moody's cut Thailand's foreign currency ceilings for bonds and bank deposits to A3 from A2 in April.
At the time, Moody's cited an incremental worsening in creditworthiness stemming from a number of factors.
Ironically, S&P's review comes just one day after Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand raised US$500 million through an issue featuring credit clauses.
The clauses stipulated that if IFCT was downgraded by two notches, the coupon would step up 50 basis points, and by 25 basis points for every subsequent single notch fall thereafter.
Investors could put the paper back to the borrower if its rating fell below investment grade.
In other news, Hanil Bank launched a US$100 million three-year floating-rate note through Lehman Brothers.
The issue was priced at 99.975 to yield 20 basis points over the three-month London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR), but carries a put exercisable in November 1997.
If the put is not exercised in November, the coupon rises to LIBOR plus 45 basis points.

A banker close to the deal said the clause was there to reassure investors reluctant to commit themselves for three years, because they wanted to see if more bad news was due out of Korea in the next few months.
But the higher LIBOR plus 45 basis points if the put is not exercised shows how the cost of funds has risen for Korean banks as well as Thai banks, bankers said.
In mid-July, Hanil bank paid 45 basis points over three-month LIBOR for a five-year FRN arranged by HSBC Markets.
India's second largest term lending, the Industrial Credit and Investment Corp of India (ICICI) joined the ranks of yankee issuers overnight Thursday with a US$150 million 10-year bond.
ICICI said 70 percent of the issue ended up in U.S. hands, 20 percent in Europe and the rest in Asia.
S&P assigned a BB foreign-currency rating to Guangzhou- Shenzhen Superhighway (Holdings) Ltd's offering of US$600 million notes.
